items.title: 1. Your MDMA section: who is most at risk of low sodium, and how to tell
items.question:
Your note on round 50: "it shows that MDMA can cause dangerous hyponatremia in something like 1/4 of people at a festival even when they take one average dose, with women being most at risk by far in this study, but not in other studies". What the study found ([van Dijken 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23476039/)): at one rave, 14% of those who took MDMA had low sodium, about one in four women and 3% of men, all of it mild. Your review's title says the rest: "Rare but relevant". So I'd say one in four women, mildly, rather than one in four people, dangerously.
Your "strong broth" holds up: the wilderness medicine guidelines replace salt by mouth with bouillon cubes or ramen seasoning in a little water, after stopping the water ([AAFP](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0215/p252.html)).
Two sentences of mine after your water sentence, and your review linked on "sodium dropping too low" (the paragraph reads [Human High as one window](https://www.pangram.com/history/cc7b7331-932e-420d-bb42-4a8201641f8d)):
"Low sodium seems to hit women hardest: at [one rave](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23476039/), about one in four women who took MDMA had a mild case, against 3% of men. If they've drunk a lot and feel bloated but not thirsty, too much water is the likely problem, so stop the water and give them something salty ([wilderness medicine guidelines](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0215/p252.html))."
A fresh reader paused at your next sentence, with "vomiting won't stop" as a reason to call and salty food "if they're alert and not vomiting", unsure whether to feed them or call. It is two cases (worse confusion or headache without vomiting: salty food while you wait), and it reads Human High, so I left it.
In, or not?
items.comment:
well gpt actually said other reviews show that men and women have the same risk so idk about that part

the exercise guidance doesn't fully apply to mdma because people on mdma can feel thirsty even when they need salt, which is why we always advise people at raves not to drink regular water but take it with electrolytes. there's no way to for sure know who has hyponatremia without testing their blood, but i think gpt gave the guidance that makes sense like have they been sweating a lot, drinking water without salt, etc, and i'm also not sure a little salty snack will do much considering the guidelines said 3g of salt in 100mL water IV'd 3x over half an hour in US. 

i'd also just blanket warn people not to dance on mdma because real mdma doesn't give you any energy to dance so i'm highly suspicious that contains amphetamines or it's not real mdma maybe 6apb or something idk or some strange way of making mdma, but i already know there are people who will be taking whatever this stuff is (often called "ecstasy")

items.title: 2. Step 8: what could harm, with almost none of the harmalas?
items.question: Step 8 says: "I'd also leave out this guide's Syrian rue oil for now: made at home it has almost none of the harmala alkaloids, but I couldn't find any research on it with MDMA, so it could help or harm here." Readers stop at "almost none" followed by "could help or harm": if there is almost none, what could harm? On round 49 you said "potentially helpful, potentially harmful with mdma", and if used, cautiously, raising the dose slowly. Which harm do you have in mind: a trace of the harmalas, which act like an MAOI, on top of MDMA; something else in the oil; or no known harm, only no research? Your answer decides the words, and whether step 8 still says to leave it out; I'll write them and check them.
items.comment:
it has almost none of the strong MAOi harmala alkaloids, but it does have plenty of harmala alkaloids so we shouldn't say it has almost none of the harmala alkaloids. also unclear why you are tlalking about harmala alkaloid. there is just no research on this so that's the main reason i'm cautious about it but the obvious danger is not there (it doesn't inhibit MAO, which is what normally makes syrian rue tea dangerous with MDMA). it makes trips (including ayahuasca) much less intense and easier to handle, so that's why i might try it as a last resort for SS if nothing else is helping and no medics are coming or something like that. 

and then you're talking about magnesium chloride again? is that the 3rd or 4th time?

items.title: 3. Quiz 3, optional: my reading of my first tries, before Pangram
items.question:
Only if you think the quiz is worth your time (my answer is in the chat). These are my first tries of this round's lines, read by three fresh readers and fixed, then read by me before any Pangram check, on purpose. The API checks changed several of them after, so the guide now has later versions; your score of these readings still tells me where my reading misses. Score each reading right or wrong ("S3 wrong: ...").
S1 (step 5): "But if they feel a strong urge to keep moving (akathisia), I'd have them tap their fingertips on their head instead (the Emotional Freedom Technique), which can soothe that urge without the over-activity risk."
My reading: not sure, "instead" ties it to the pacing just ruled out, and each term comes after its plain words, but two asides in brackets in one sentence may read like terms dropped in.
S2 (step 6): "That can be as simple as a salty potato broth with some magnesium chloride flakes stirred in, since potatoes are full of potassium."
My reading: not sure, "That" ties it and the broth comes first, your idea with its reason, but a reader waiting for an ambulance may not have time to cook potatoes, and "some" is still no amount.
S3 (step 6): "If you don't have the flakes, Epsom salt works too, although it causes diarrhea more easily."
My reading: reads right, the tie at the start answers what the reader will ask next, then your trade-off.
S4 (step 6): "Whatever you give, give it slowly to see how it affects them, since their potassium could be running low or high: MDMA can drain it, but muscles breaking down into the blood can push it up."
My reading: not sure, the act comes first, your "slowly", and the reason says which way potassium goes, as you asked, but the colon packs both directions after the act.
S5 (step 6): "So I'd stick to food like the potato broth for potassium, since too much pure potassium is dangerous for anyone."
My reading: reads right, "So" ties it to the line before, the act first, and the reason is the one you gave.
S6 (step 8): "DMSO, though, seems to help prevent seizures, so if there's any sign of an overdose, I'd start by having them smell it, or rub a little on a clean patch of skin, mixed with about 30% water if it makes the skin itch."
My reading: not sure, "though" ties it to niacin and the reason comes first, your order, but the sentence carries a condition and two ways to give it with a third condition on the second.
S7 (step 8): "Then I'd use more, a little at a time, as long as it seems to help, since seizures have happened when a lot of DMSO went straight into the blood with stem cell infusions."
My reading: not sure, "Then" ties it, but the reason is a hospital case far from a skin rub, and the reader has to work out why it means going slowly.
S8 (step 8): "Magnesium chloride is the other one I'd use, since many people with serotonin syndrome run low on magnesium."
My reading: reads right, "the other one" ties it to DMSO, the round-49 line with the one word that changed.
S9 (step 8): "If they're not able to swallow, I'd rub magnesium chloride on their skin instead, dissolved in a little water, or Epsom salt if that's all you have, though Epsom salt gets through the skin less well."
My reading: not sure, the condition is the reader's case and the act comes right after it, but three additions follow the act.
S10 (MDMA: Magnesium Alarm): "Women are most at risk of this: at one rave, about one in four women who took MDMA had low sodium, against 3% of men."
My reading: reads right, "of this" ties it to the low sodium just named, the claim first and then the numbers that show it.
S11 (MDMA: Magnesium Alarm): "To tell whether too much water is the problem, ask whether they've drunk a lot, and look for bloating, puffy hands, or rings that feel tight."
My reading: not sure, the purpose opens the sentence, which says why to read on, but it delays the act by eight words.
